title: He Who has Turned a Hero-stone
paragraphs: The wars waged by the ancient Tamils to either capture the cows or to retrieve the cows were fought with codes of conduct. From which direction is he throwing the spear or for that matter, from which direction is he shooting the arrows? In the event of the warrors confronting each other in the warfield, what was the method employed to distinguish between our men and the enemy?

> Wearing of palmyra, morgosa and mountain ebony, > The [totemic] flowers of towering note, > That mark identity and distinctiveness > Among soldiers who make the massive armies > Which the great monarchs of burning hostility commanded.
To distinguish between the enemy and one’s own soldiers, during face-to-face confrontation, the soldiers were made to wear the garlands of male palmyra tree, neem tree and common mountain ebony tree.
> Rout of foemen in a fierce battle; > Recovery of the cows captured;

> Singing the praises of the monarch of lasting note; > The warrior taking lofty vows > On account of his exceeding prowess in war; > Apart from these > Which the karaṇtai theme characterizes, > The others proper to veṭci are: > The twofold piḷḷainilai of > Resisting the vanguard of the opposing army > And being felled by the enemy’s sword; > The people rejoicing at the valour of the warrior > Who withstood the strike of the enemy’s sword, > To the accompaniment of drum-beat, > And bestowing the land on him; > The choice of the proper stone > For erecting the memorial of the fallen warrior; > Commencing the sculpturing of the dead warrior’s image; > Giving the stone a ceremonial bathing; > Erecting the stone thus sculptured; > Bestowing honours right in accord with tradition; > And praise and worship extended to the stone. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 5)
What follows is an imaginative illustration of this Tolkāppiyam exposition:

They made the enemy run for cover showing their back. The cows captured by the veṭci soliders were retrieved. They trumpeted and hailed their king for his deft strategy which fed valour and strength, culminating in a glorious victory.
The veṭci soldiers boasted that cows captured by them could not be retrieved, just as milk - the food from the udder of cows - cannot be restored to the cows.

But our king shattered all the tall claims of these warriors. Thus they hailed their king and sang hosannas about him. In the meantime, the prince in the prime of his youth thundered, “O king, issue your command! In order to sing accolades of our victory not merely confining to retrieval of the cows but for the act of capturing the entire lot of enemy’s land, issue command unto me. I would shatter the strong fort of the enemy and ruin the front ranks of the army, which guard that land. I will make the enemy subservient to us, through the might of my sword. I salute and await your orders, with a vow to accomplish this task. You nourished
me affectionately during my childhood days. Now, I am a grown-up man, how can you be afraid of issuing orders?” He spoke in a voice, which sounded like an explosion.

“I am proud of parenting a brave son. My arms swell up in excitement, to see you stand seeking permission, with a sword in your hand. My heart quivers in excitement. Yes, proceed towards the fort. Annihilate all the wings of foe’s army, be it the front rank, cavalry, infantry or the elephant wing. You have obtained the permission, dear prince. March on!”
After getting the king’s permission, the elite wing of the army raised the war cry “Victory is ours” and marched forward to the beating of the drums.

The doors of the fort got shattered! The flag pole fell down! With nobody left to save the country, the nation of veṭci men became a virtual hunted ground for the karaṇtai warriors. “We are unparalleled” was the song on the lips of the karaṇtai soldiers.
The prince raised the sword, which fetched victory to him and his army and entered the fort riding his horse. At the time of entry, a spear flying from nowhere pierced through his chest.
He held the fatal spear and breathed his last, but not before accounting for ten to twenty heads of the enemy soldiers.

“Dear son! You declined the golden crown and rather chose the aura of fame through bravery,” a visibly perturbed king kissed his forehead. The soldiers, unable to celebrate their victory fully, erected a hero-stone for the immortal prince in tune with the practice of raising hero-stones in memory of the warriors dying undaunted in the field of battle.
